1:
The psalm opens not at the sanctuary door but over the whole created order, and the witnesses gather first about the sweep of its opening claim, that "the earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof, the world, and they that dwell therein." The reformed John Gill takes the fulness for the whole terraqueous globe — land and water and circumambient air, the fish of the sea, the fowl of the air, the beasts of the field, the plants that spring from the ground, and the metals and minerals in the bowels of it — all of it the riches of the Lord. His fellow reformed voice John Calvin grants that under "fulness" all the riches with which the earth is adorned are comprehended, as Paul's authority proves, yet has no doubt the Psalmist intends chiefly men themselves, who are the most illustrious ornament and glory of the earth; strip the earth of them and it were a scene of desolation, for to what end are so many fruits produced in such abundance, and so many pleasant countries, if not for the use and comfort of men?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the note of ownership into a doctrine of stewardship: when God gave the earth to the children of men he reserved to himself the property and only let it out to them as tenants, so that what falls to our share is but lent, the Lord's still, and wherever a child of God goes he does not go off his Father's ground. C.H. Spurgeon, of the same puritan-evangelical school, turns the verse against every narrowing of grace, rebuking the notion that the holy land alone was God's and Abraham's seed his only people: the whole round world is claimed for Jehovah, and Christ has made an end of the exclusiveness of nationalities, so that the meanest dweller in the world belongs to him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the Sovereign Ruler of the universe, Creator and Governor, whose the soil is though men parcel out its kingdoms; and he sets the psalm at the bringing of the ark from the house of Obed-edom to Mount Zion. The grammatical-historical witnesses fasten on Paul's use of the line: Keil and Delitzsch note that in 1 Cor. 10:26 the apostle founds on it the liberty to eat whatever is sold in the shambles, and record the Talmudic teacher who drew from it the duty of prayer before meat, since he who eats without giving thanks lays hands on the sacred things of God; Charles Ellicott adds that the majesty of Jehovah as Lord of the universe is itself the psalmist's reason for demanding rectitude in his worshippers. The latin-fathers Augustine of Hippo reads the whole from the height of the resurrection, taking the psalm of the Lord glorified early on the first day of the week, the compass of the world become his Church, founded above the seas that their waves might be subdued, and prepared above the rivers, that the lusts which flow into the world might be overcome.
2:
The ground of that universal ownership is laid, the witnesses observe, in the work of creation itself, "for he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods." The reformed John Gill weighs the preposition, reading it as founded "upon" or "with" or "by" the seas — the earth and the seas made together and both established upon nothing, yet firm — and recalls the old conjecture that the first earth stood over the waters as a crust or shell, until the deluge broke it in and formed the sea. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the plain wonder of the thing: God not only created the vast mass but separated the land from the waters, so that the mountains, raised above the flood, appear to be founded on it, and for all the ragings of the ocean these waters cannot prevail; the earth is established and cannot be shaken. John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, takes the seas for the whole collection of waters — the sea and the rivers that run into it, and that great abyss of waters contained in the bowels of the earth.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the image among its kindred passages — the earth resting on the water of Ps. 136:6 and Prov. 8:25-29 — and marks that in Genesis the dry land emerges from the water but is not said to be founded on it, while in Job 26:7 the earth is hung upon nothing; the notion of a water-foundation, he suggests, grew naturally from the phenomenon of springs before it was scientifically explained. His fellow grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, hear the festal procession by this point arriving above at the gates of the citadel, and look ahead to the "everlasting doors" of the antiphon, insisting they be rendered doors of eternity and not, as Luther had it, doors "of the world."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds three things in the ground of God's title. He made the earth, forming it out of nothing and fitting it for man's use, so that none can lay claim to any part but from and under him; he made it as none else could, the creature of omnipotence, for a foundation of seas and floods seems a weak and unstable thing to bear the weight of a world, and yet at almighty pleasure it serves; and he continues it, having so established it that, though one generation passes and another comes, the earth abides (Eccl. 1:4). Yet the very floods beneath it, Henry adds, should remind us how slippery and uncertain all earthly things are, their foundation not sand only but water, so that it is our folly to build upon them.
3:
From the breadth of the earth the psalm turns, of a sudden, to a single steep question, and the witnesses climb with it: "who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? who shall stand in his holy place?" The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry feels the meditation rise from this world to another, whose foundation is not on the seas nor on the floods; a soul that knows its own immortal nature, having viewed the earth and its fulness, sits down unsatisfied and asks what it must do to rise toward God, toward heaven, to the hill where the Lord dwells and manifests himself. The hill of Zion, Henry says, typified the church, both visible and invisible, and the question is much the same as that of Ps. 15:1. C.H. Spurgeon, of the same puritan-evangelical school, calls it uphill work for the creature to reach the Creator, and hears the true Israel described, a company marked not by race but by character, a chosen people made meet to dwell in the holy hill; and he presses the second clause, "who shall stand," as asking who can continue there, since God casts away the wicked and none may gaze upon the Holy One and abide in the blaze of his glory but by grace.

The reformed John Gill, though he allows the reference to Mount Moriah and the hill of Zion where the temple would stand, takes the church to be mystically intended — so called for its visibility, through the profession of faith in Christ, and for its immovableness, being built on him. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses keep the question nearer the sanctuary: Adam Clarke reads it of who is sufficiently holy to wait in God's temple and fit to minister in the holy place, and John Wesley takes the hill for Zion or Moriah, the place of God's sanctuary and special presence, and "stand" for the posture of ministers and servants — who, that is, shall serve God with his acceptation.

Here the witnesses genuinely divide over the height the question measures. Gill, Henry, and Spurgeon read the ascent as the soul's climb to communion with God in grace now and glory hereafter, the hill a figure of the church and of heaven itself; Clarke and Wesley keep it to the literal holiness required of those who would minister in the earthly sanctuary and stand before the ark. The difference is not a quarrel over the fact that God requires clean worshippers, but over whether the "hill" is the temple-mount of the liturgy or the heavenly Zion of which it was the type — and the witnesses hold the two together as readily as they distinguish them, the one ascent shadowing the other.
4:
The answer to who may ascend names neither birth nor rank but a fourfold character, and the witnesses take its clauses in turn: "he that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully." The reformed John Gill notes that though clean hands are named first, as the more visible, the pure heart is first in being and in order, the fountain from which clean hands flow; and since no man has a pure heart naturally — the heart being desperately wicked — it is God who creates the clean heart and purifies it by faith, so that from that inward purity comes the outward, the clean hands that signify a holy and harmless conversation, the washing of the hands being the old token of innocence. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads clean hands of an irreproachable conscience and the pure heart of one without deceit and unruled by unholy passion, while to have "not lifted up his soul unto vanity" is to have no idolatrous inclination, a pure faith that conscientiously keeps its engagements. John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, glosses the pure heart as careful to approve itself to God as well as to men, ordering the very thoughts and affections by God's word, and takes "vanity" of the vain things of this life — honours, riches, pleasures — which such a man does not value nor desire, but makes God his portion.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings the philology. The Hebrew margin reads "my soul" for "his soul," a reading the Alexandrian Codex of the Septuagint confirms, and which the Rabbis defend by taking soul for "name" (comparing Amos 6:8 and Jer. 51:14), so that to lift up the soul to vanity becomes to take the name in vain. "Vanity" itself he reads, from the parallelism, in the sense of falsehood, as in Job 31:5; and "deceitfully" is literally "to fraud," from a root meaning to trip up. He notes too that the Septuagint and Vulgate add, from Ps. 15, the words "to his neighbour."

The latin-fathers Augustine of Hippo reads the character spiritually and toward eternity: the guiltless in deed and pure in thought is the one who "hath not received his soul in vain," who has not reckoned his soul among the things that pass away but, feeling it immortal, has longed for an eternity steadfast and unchangeable, and who therefore, like the things eternal that are simple and undeceiving, has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbour. The witnesses do not divide over the substance, agreeing that the ascent is barred to none by birth and opened to none by mere ritual, but is for the clean of hand and pure of heart alone.
5:
Such a one climbs not to earn but to receive, and the witnesses mark the turn from requirement to gift: "he shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation." The reformed John Gill reads the future as a present — "who receives" — and continues the portrait of the man fit to enter and abide in the church of God: one who has received every spiritual blessing in Christ, special grace out of his fulness, and in particular the blessing of pardon, together with adoption and a right to eternal life; the "righteousness" of the next clause he takes as the very substance of that blessing, perhaps explanatory of it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose comment on these verses runs together, unfolds the privileges into a chain: God's peculiar people shall be blessed, receiving all the fruits and gifts of his favour according to his promise, for whom God blesses are blessed indeed; they shall be justified and sanctified, receiving that righteousness which they hunger and thirst after (Matt. 5:6); and they shall be saved, for God himself will be the God of their salvation — where God gives righteousness, Henry adds, he certainly designs salvation, and those made meet for heaven shall be brought safely to it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in "the blessing" a possible allusion to Obed-edom, at whose house the ark had lodged and on whom God had poured especial blessings; and he reads the "righteousness" as mercy — every kind of necessary good — since it is God's mercy that crowns the obedience and fidelity of good men, the same mercy that first made them good and faithful. John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, keeps the sense broad, taking "the blessing" for grace and glory and all other good things.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes on the second noun as the heart of the verse: righteousness is the real blessing that comes from God. That virtue is her own reward, he says, is the moral statement of the truth; the highest religious statement of it must be looked for in Christ's Beatitudes. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the reward held out to the clean of hand is not of debt but of grace, a blessing and a righteousness alike received from the God of his salvation — so that the very holiness demanded at the gate is confessed, in the receiving of it, to be his gift and not the climber's achievement, and the man made meet for the hill is brought at last to the God who made him meet.
6:
The psalm gathers this whole company of the clean and the receiving into one description, and the witnesses weigh it: "this is the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob." The reformed John Gill takes the generation for the children of God, who in every age are accounted by him for a generation, and who seek him in the first place and with their whole hearts, and seek him in Christ, where alone he is to be found. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in it a praying people — in every age a remnant of such, accounted to the Lord for a generation (Ps. 22:30) — who both join themselves to God, seeking his favour in earnest prayer and serious endeavour to keep within his love, and join themselves to the people of God, coming into the communion of saints; for all who strive in prayer are the spiritual seed of Jacob, to whom God never said, Seek ye me in vain.

Over the last clause the witnesses openly contend, for it strains the grammar. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke holds that the divine name has dropped from the text: "Elohey, O God," is wanting in most Hebrew manuscripts but preserved in two of Kennicott's and in the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon, so that the line should run "who seek thy face, O God of Jacob"; and "Selah" he takes for a mark of confirmation — it is true. John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, reads the generation as the true progeny God regards and "face" as his grace and favour, his own margin likewise supplying "O God of Jacob." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees flatly that the address "O Jacob" is certainly wrong, and that many critics, following the Septuagint and Syriac, rightly insert "O God of."

So the sides are drawn over a single missing word. Some, with Clarke, Ellicott, and Wesley's margin, mend the text after the ancient versions and read "the God of Jacob," the object of the people's seeking; others, keeping the received text, hear Jacob himself named — the patriarch who wrestled and prevailed, sought God and found him — as the pattern of every seeker, so that to seek God's face is to seek it as Jacob did, a reading Henry entertains even while he notes the marginal "O God of Jacob." The witnesses do not divide over the thing sought, the face and favour of God; they divide only over whether the verse names the seeker's God, or the seeking patriarch whose very name became Israel.
7:
"Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in." With the great antiphon at the gates the psalm changes key, and the witnesses divide at once over what gates these are. The reformed John Gill sets aside the readings he thinks false — that they are the gates of hell, opened at Christ's descent to fetch the fathers from a supposed limbus, or even, strictly, the gates of heaven — and follows the Jewish interpreters who understand the gates of the temple, David prophesying their opening when Solomon should build and dedicate the house and the ark, the symbol of Jehovah's presence, be carried in. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the words as the shout of those who precede the ark, an allusion to the triumphal entry of a victorious general into the imperial city, and even sets beside them two lines of Callimachus's hymn to Apollo — "Fall back, ye bolts; ye pond'rous doors, give way" — while taking the "everlasting doors" for a portcullis hung by pulleys, bidden to be lifted that so august a Personage may enter. John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, sees the doors of the temple, beheld by prophecy as already built, and calls them everlasting not for durable materials but in opposition to the tabernacle, which was removed from place to place.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott recovers the poetry the versions had blunted: the Septuagint and Vulgate miss the fine personification by rendering "princes" for "heads," and the antiquarian "portcullis" is scarcely more excusable; the poet deems the ancient gateways of the conquered Jebusite castle too low for the dignity of the approaching Monarch, and calls on them to open wide and high. "Everlasting doors" he would render "ancient doors, gates of old," fitting the grim old fortress venerable with unconquered age, and hears in "the King of glory" that glory which fled with the cry Ichabod now returning to seek a lasting resting-place.

But the puritan-evangelical witnesses lift the antiphon from the ark to Christ. Matthew Henry, granting that the entry refers first to the bringing of the ark into the tent or temple, doubtless points it at the ascension of Christ, who, having by his blood made atonement, demanded entrance as the forerunner at those everlasting doors once shut against us (Gen. 3:24), the angels asking in wonder, Who is this King of glory? C.H. Spurgeon, of the same puritan-evangelical school, sees the great representative Man rising from Olivet, the cloud receiving him and the attending spirits calling on the everlasting gates to give way before one higher than the heavens. So the debate stands: whether the gates are the temple's, flung open for the ark's entry into Zion, or heaven's, opened for the ascending Christ — a division the witnesses hold not as contradiction but as type and fulfilment.
8:
The demand at the gate is answered from within by a challenge, and the witnesses attend to the antiphon's question and its reply: "who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle." The reformed John Gill hears the question put by the church, or by particular believers — not through ignorance, as the daughters of Jerusalem or the Pharisees, nor in the pride and scorn of a Pharaoh, but as wondering at the glories and excellencies of Christ's person and desirous of knowing more of him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole as a dialogue: those without demand entrance, those within ask who this glorious King may be, and the answer comes that it is Jehovah, come to set up his abode in his imperial city, who has conquered his enemies and brought salvation to Israel. Clarke presses further into a resurrection reading — that Jesus, having by dying conquered sin, Satan, and death, now rises and, as a mighty Conqueror, claims entrance into the realm of glory he purchased by his blood, "the Lord mighty in battle" by his victory and "the Lord of hosts" in respect of the followers he will raise. John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, keeps the answer plain: the Lord is no ordinary person, no other than Jehovah, who has subdued all his enemies and is now returned in triumph.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott feels the drama of the reluctant gates: the claim is not unchallenged, for the old heathen gates will not at once recognise the new-comer's right of admission, and the title by which it is pressed is the right of conquest — "Jehovah, the strong, the mighty, Jehovah, mighty in battle." His fellow grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, simply set out the answering verses of the antiphon, letting the challenge and its threefold naming of the warrior King stand as the psalm gives them.

Here the witnesses differ chiefly in reach rather than in substance. Gill and Wesley and Ellicott keep to the scene at the gate, the warrior Jehovah demanding entrance for his ark; Clarke alone carries the "mighty in battle" beyond the field to the empty tomb, hearing in the challenged entry the risen Christ claiming the heavens he had won. The witnesses do not quarrel over the King's identity — all name him Jehovah of the armies, strong to save — but only over whether the battle in view is Israel's deliverance or the great conquest of death itself.
9:
The whole antiphon now begins again, gate and door summoned a second time — "lift up your heads, O ye gates, even lift them up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in" — and the witnesses ask why the psalm repeats itself. The reformed John Gill finds the reason in the backwardness and negligence of churches and of particular believers to open and let Christ in, as with the church that kept him standing and knocking at the door (Rev. 3:20); the summons is doubled, too, the more to set forth the greatness and glory of the Christ about to make his entrance, and to command a proper awe of him. Some, Gill notes, take the two liftings-up for the twofold coming of Christ — first into the second temple, and again at the last judgment — though he himself thinks the certainty of his spiritual coming to his church and people the thing chiefly designed.

John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, reads the repetition as spoken to awaken the dulness of mankind, so hardly brought to a serious preparation for such solemnities, and to signify the great importance of the matter carried under the words. His fellow wesleyan-arminian voice, Adam Clarke, following the dialogue of the antiphon, marks that those within do not at once obey the first summons, so that the demand must be raised a second time before a yet more particular question is put and answered.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, hearing the same reiteration across the closing verses, observes that what is spoken once is spoken a second time, as is usual in songs, and with much beauty in it: entrance is demanded again for the King of glory, the doors thrown wide once more because he stands and knocks, ready to come in and take possession as the rightful owner after the title has long been contested. God in his word and ordinances is thus to be welcomed, Henry adds, with great readiness — the doors flung open that the word of the Lord may come into the innermost and uppermost place of the soul — and with all reverence, remembering how great a God he is with whom we have to do in every approach to him. The witnesses do not divide. Whether the repetition serves to shame the slowness of the heart that will not open, to rouse a dull and unready world, or simply to heighten by a solemn echo the majesty of the coming King, all hear in the doubled cry one purpose — that the everlasting doors be flung open without reserve, and the King of glory be welcomed in.
10:
"Who is this King of glory?" The challenge from the gate is raised a second time, and the witnesses hear the antiphon come to its rest in the last and greatest of the King's names: "the LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory." The reformed John Gill reads the repeated question as asked in order to draw out a fuller account of his glorious Person, the church desiring to know yet more of him than the first answer had told. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in it a second challenge from the reluctant gates, which serves to inaugurate the great name by which the divine nature was especially known under the monarchy, the LORD of hosts — a name whose origin and force he sends the reader to trace at 1 Sam. 1:3.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks how the very form of the question has shifted between the two askings: at v.8 it was "who is this King of glory," asked before the ark appeared, when his coming was but announced; here it is "who is He, this King of glory," the wording altered because the ark, the symbol of the divine Presence, has now arrived — "here He is, to answer for himself" — whereupon, we may suppose, the portcullis was lifted, the gates thrown open, and the whole procession admitted. Though the psalm has all the appearance of an unfinished piece, Clarke owns, there is in it a vast deal of dignity and majesty, the demands from without, the questions from within, and the answers to them all partaking of the true sublime, where nature, dignity, and simplicity are judiciously mingled; and he closes the scene with the word of the prophet, "The Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him." John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, unfolds the title itself: the Lord "of hosts" is he under whose command are all the armies of heaven and earth, angels and men and every other creature.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott and Clarke and Wesley alike hear the psalm close where its whole movement had been tending — the gates flung wide at last, and the entering King named not merely strong and mighty in battle but the LORD of hosts, sovereign of every army in heaven and on earth, so that the liturgy which opened by claiming the earth and its fulness ends by bringing the earth's Maker home in triumph through the ancient doors of his own city. The great name is the answer to the great question, and the procession halts a moment to let it stand before the gates close behind the King.
